sources.title: The Use of Salt in Aquaculture
Aquarium Salt: When and How to Use It Properly
Garlic keeps fanged fish parasites away
Cách phòng bệnh cá La Hán trong mùa lạnh.
Salt Tolerance in the Callichthyid Catfish (Corydoras aeneus)

facts.fact: Long-lasting stress severely weakens the fish immune system, which gives pathogens more chances to cause disease.
Cold stress can completely stop the activity of the immune system's 'killer cells'.
UF/IFAS frames disease prevention as good management: good water quality, good nutrition and sanitation.
Poor nutrition can cause poor growth, deformities, a depressed immune system, hepatic lipidosis and impaired metabolism.
Fish need ascorbic acid (vitamin C) delivered in their feed, and most fish foods should contain a stabilized form of it.
Merck recommends adding vitamins to fish diets, including vitamin E, vitamin B1 and stabilized vitamin C.
Vitamin C deficiency is called 'broken back disease' by some farmers and hobbyists. Severe cases show extreme scoliosis.
Milder vitamin C deficiency can show as bent or deformed gill cartilage, seen on a wet mount of gill tissue under a 10× objective.
Hepatic lipidosis can result from starvation, a diet too high in carbohydrate or lipid, or rancid feed.
Store dry feed in a pest-proof container in a cool, low-humidity place. Heat and humidity degrade the diet, promote mold and possible mycotoxins, and cause rancidity.
Discard an opened feed container kept at room temperature after 2 months, and commercial feed stored in the freezer after 6 months.
Commercial frozen foods (brine shrimp, bloodworms, mysids, glassworms) should be discarded after 1 year. Thawed frozen feed should not be refrozen.
Combining live feeds with varied commercial feeds helps meet nutritional needs and keeps fish from eating only one food type.
Adult fish need about 3% of body weight in food daily for maintenance, and fry and fingerlings up to 5%.
Leaving pellets to dissolve in the water before fish eat them pollutes the water.
A 3 percent salt dip removes protozoa from the skin, gills and fins of freshwater fish and increases mucus production.
If a dip is not feasible, freshwater fish may be kept in a 1 percent salt (brackish water) solution for 30 minutes up to several hours.
Using too little salt makes a salt treatment ineffective. The concentration has to match the treatment's duration.
Aquarium Co-Op's level 1 salt dose is 1 Tbsp per 3 gallons, used for 4–5 days for mild bacterial and fungal infections, then increased if there is no improvement.
Aquarium Co-Op's level 2 salt dose is 1 Tbsp per 2 gallons. It is used for 10 days against ich, with the dose raised if symptoms worsen after 5 days.
Aquarium Co-Op's level 3 salt dose is 1 Tbsp per 1 gallon, kept for when lower levels fail. It is very hard on sensitive fish.
Aquarium Co-Op suggests salt level 1 (1 Tbsp per 3 gallons) for 2 weeks during quarantine.
To end a salt treatment once fish look healthy, do a 30% water change without salt and watch for a week. Then do another 30% unsalted change and watch for another week.
Salt does not evaporate or filter out. During treatment, replace only the share removed by a water change (for a 20% change, add 20% of the original dose).
Most live aquarium plants and most snails cannot tolerate aquarium salt. Anchor catfish cannot take even Aquarium Co-Op's level 1.
Scaleless fish and other sensitive species struggle at salt level 3. Caridina crystal shrimp have not been tested.
Aquarium Co-Op lists rasboras, danios, tetras, silver dollars, livebearers, most cichlids (including fry) and Neocaridina cherry shrimp as fairly tolerant of level 3 salt.
Use plain aquarium salt or NaCl rock salt, not table salt, marine salt or Epsom salt.
Overdosing salt can kill everything in the tank, not just the pathogens.
Using salt daily as a preventative can lead to resistant diseases, according to Aquarium Co-Op.
Aquarium Co-Op calls it a myth that fish need salt daily for electrolytes, and says to use salt only when needed.
Aquarium Co-Op says salt is not a cure-all, because some microorganisms withstand higher salinity.
A study on Corydoras aeneus tested salt tolerance and considered 1.0–2.0 ppt therapeutic, but it used artificial sea salt.
In a James Cook University study, barramundi were fed garlic-enriched diets for 30 days before exposure to the marine flatworm parasite Neobenedenia.
Half the garlic-fed barramundi stayed completely free of infection, while 100% of fish on the unenriched diet became infected.
The barramundi ate more of the garlic-enriched feed, unlike bitter commercial treatments that fish often spit out.
NippyFish found no solid scientific backing for garlic in aquarium fish. The popular claim traces to a 1999 Tropical Fish Hobbyist report on parasite-infected discus.
In that report, discus fed garlic-oil-soaked food had fewer internal parasites after 6 weeks. Fresh garlic puree reduced parasites over 5 weeks but did not kill the worms.
NippyFish says the idea that garlic stimulates appetite probably grew from one article saying discus ate the treated food 'eagerly'.
NippyFish says Seachem's Garlic Guard is marketed as an appetite and flavor enhancer, not as a medicine.
Forum contributors quoted by NippyFish said garlic cannot cure fin rot directly.
NippyFish warns that garlic is toxic to many animals (dogs, cats, birds) and only tentatively suggests a conservative dose is safe for fish.
Several keepers commenting on NippyFish reported that their bettas refused garlic-treated food.
A Vietnamese flowerhorn (cá La Hán) keeper says moving from 32–33°C in summer to 27–28°C at the season change can trigger fungal problems.
The same keeper keeps the tank at 30°C during the season change, then lowers it gradually to about 28°C.
The keeper suggests about 200–300 W of heater for 60–100 L tanks and 300–600 W for 100–250 L tanks.
The keeper warns that a cold-weather water change can drop tank temperature 3–4°C when outdoor temperatures reach 6–7°C, so new water should be warmed first.
During the season change, the keeper changes 20% of the water twice a week, keeps each change to 15% or less, and insulates the tank.
